title: fix: avoid wrapping pseudo-element selectors in :is() during nesting compilation
author: donlion
summary: Lowers `.element::after { .parent & {} }` to `.parent .element:after`, so the rule matches. Per the nesting spec `&` can't represent pseudo-elements, and Chromium matches nothing here, so the PR would make the compiled CSS style something browsers don't. The maintainer's multi-selector concern was never resolved. The right direction is #982 (don't lower or match nothing), not this.
evidence: Chromium 153 with native nesting: `.element::after{content:"x"; .parent & {color:red}}` -> ::after color stays rgb(0,0,0) (rule matches nothing). master 574eee2 CLI with no targets: passes through unchanged. devongovett 2026-03-09: "what happens if there are multiple selectors? ... doing this without `:is` is really difficult if not impossible in some cases to do correctly." yisibl (member) 2026-03-09: spec doesn't permit `&` to represent pseudo-elements; see #975 comment and WPT nesting-basic. Author asked for direction; no reply since. Open issue #982 covers the spec-correct fix.
draft:
Thanks for looking into this! It turns out browsers treat this case differently than it might seem: the nesting selector `&` can't represent a pseudo-element, so in Chrome with native nesting, `.element::after { .parent & { color: red } }` doesn't match anything and the `::after` stays unstyled. Compiling it to `.parent .element:after` would make it red, so the output would behave differently from the source. Since the nested rule can't match anything, the right fix is the other way around: don't lower it to something that matches (tracked in #982), rather than unwrapping the `:is()`. I'm going to close this one, but thanks again for digging into the nesting code!
